objectives.label: Basic circle terms and radii
objectives.description: Identify and use the basic terms of the circle (centre, radius, chord, diameter, surface of the circle, points inside, on and outside) and use radii and diameters to compare lengths and solve problems.

objectives.label: Axes of symmetry in circle
objectives.description: Describe the axes of symmetry of a circle and state that any straight line through the centre is an axis of symmetry.

objectives.label: Chord–centre perpendicular corollaries
objectives.description: Apply the corollaries relating the centre, a chord and its midpoint or perpendicular to calculate lengths, angles and areas and to prove statements about chords.

entries.text: Photo (satellite/aerial) of green circular irrigated fields next to desert, with an irrigation machine arm.

A.why: Decorative photo introducing the lesson.

B.why: Photo of circular fields only decorates the lesson introduction.

entries.text: The circle is the set of points of a plane which are at constant distance from a fixed point in the same plane.

A.why: Defines the circle, a basic term.

B.why: Defines the circle.

entries.text: The fixed point is called the centre of the circle and the constant distance is called the radius length.

A.why: Defines centre and radius.

B.why: Defines centre and radius length.

entries.text: A circle is usually denoted by its center: circle M means the circle whose center is point M.

A.why: Naming a circle by its centre, basic circle notation.

B.why: Naming a circle by its centre, a basic term.

entries.text: Circle with centre marked as point M, shaded light green.

A.why: Shows circle with centre M.

B.why: Circle with centre M illustrating the basic terms.

entries.text: The set of points inside the circle, like points M, D, E, ...

A.why: Points inside the circle.

B.why: Points inside the circle.

entries.text: The set of points on the circle, like points A, B, C, ...

A.why: Points on the circle.

B.why: Points on the circle.

entries.text: The set of points outside the circle, like points X, Y, Z, ...

A.why: Points outside the circle.

B.why: Points outside the circle.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; points D, E inside (and M); A, B, C on the circle; X, Y, Z outside the circle.

A.why: Illustrates points inside, on and outside.

B.why: Shows points inside, on and outside the circle.

entries.text: Surface of the circle: the set of points of the circle ∪ the set of points inside the circle. $\text{circle} \cup \text{interior points}$

A.why: Defines surface of the circle.

B.why: Defines surface of the circle.

entries.text: Yellow circle with centre M; a line AB (with arrows) crosses the circle's lower part, meeting it at D and C; B and A are on the line outside the circle (B left, A right).

A.why: Line crossing the circle, points on/outside it.

B.why: Line crossing circle meeting it at two points, basic terms.

entries.text: Radius of a circle: a line segment with one endpoint at the center and the other endpoint on the circle.

A.why: Defines radius as a segment.

B.why: Defines radius.

entries.text: Two circles are congruent if their radii are equal in length.

A.why: Congruent circles compared by radii.

B.why: Congruent circles have equal radii, a radius comparison.

entries.text: Pink circle with centre M and points C (top), B (left), A (lower right) on the circle; radii MC, MB, MA drawn with tick marks showing they are equal.

A.why: Equal radii of a circle.

B.why: Radii MC, MB, MA are equal.

entries.text: Green circle with centre M and points C (top), A (upper right), D and E (left) and B (bottom right) on the circle; chord AB is drawn.

A.why: Shows a chord.

B.why: Circle with points and chord AB illustrating terms.

entries.text: Pink circle with centre M; horizontal chord BA through M (diameter); point C on the circle at top-left with segments CA and CM drawn.

A.why: Shows a diameter as a chord through the centre.

B.why: Diameter and radius figure with chord BA through centre.

entries.text: Exercise 5a: circle with centre M, points A and B on circle, triangle MAB shaded green; angle at M is X°, angle at A is 40°.

B.why: Exercise 5 isosceles triangle from two radii.

entries.text: Exercise 5b: circle centre M, chord/diameter through B and A with pink triangle MBA; angle at M marked 220° (reflex), angle at A is Y°.

B.why: Exercise 5 using equal radii in triangle MBA.

entries.text: Exercise 5c: circle centre M with diameter through B; points E, D on circle; ray from D extended to A beyond circle (with MD... tick marks on DA and MD); triangle MED with angles Y° at E side and X° at D; angle 27° at M between MD and MB.

A.why: Exercise using equal radii for angles.

B.why: Exercise 5 using equal radii.

entries.text: Exercise 5d: circle centre M with points A, B, C on circle; AB = 10 cm; angle at M marked X (between MA and MC, also X at C side); angle at B 35°; angle Y° at A.

A.why: Exercise using equal radii for angles.

B.why: Exercise 5 using equal radii.

entries.text: Exercise 5e: circle centre M with points A, B, C, D on circle; triangle MAB pink with tick marks; triangle MCD blue with angle 50° at C and tick marks; angle X° at M; angle Y° at A.

A.why: Exercise using equal radii for angles.

B.why: Exercise 5 using equal radii in triangles.

entries.text: Exercise 5f: circle centre M with vertical diameter line through D; points A, B, C on circle; angle 20° at D; angle 50° at A; angle X° at A side; angle Y° at M/B side.

A.why: Exercise using radii for angles.

B.why: Exercise 5 using radii equal to find angles.

entries.text: Green circle centre M, diameter AB horizontal, extended past A to N; D on top of circle, C on circle near A; line DC extended to N; dashed radius MD.

A.why: Exercise with diameter and radius.

B.why: Diameter, radius and chord used to compare lengths in an exercise.

entries.text: Circle M shaded pink with several straight lines through centre M, labelled L1, L2, L3, L4, L5 (subscripts hard to read); each line passes through M and has arrows at ends.

A.why: Lines through the centre as axes of symmetry.

B.why: Several lines through centre show they are axes of symmetry.

entries.text: Drill 1 A: circle M, radius MC perpendicular to chord AB at C, chord BA with tick marks on BC and CA (equal), angle at M between MC and MB marked 50°, angle at A marked with ? (angle MAC) in triangle MCA shaded blue. Values read from figure; verify.

entries.text: Drill 1 B: circle M with chord CA through E (E on chord, ME to it), points C, A, D, B on circle; angle 60° at A in green triangle A E D region; tick marks on equal chords/arcs; angle DME asked. Read from figure; verify.

entries.text: Drill 1 F: circle M with points A, B, C on circle; MD perpendicular to chord AB at D (right angle), triangle MAD pink; green triangle with angle 2X° at B region, C above B.

entries.text: Circle M with chord AB, C midpoint of AB, M joined to A, ray MC meets circle at D below; triangle ADB shaded pink. Points M, C, A, B, D labelled.

A.why: Midpoint of chord joined to centre.

B.why: C midpoint of chord, line MC perpendicular to chord, used in proof.

entries.text: Two concentric circles with centre M; chord BA of larger circle meets smaller circle at D and C; E is the foot of the perpendicular from M to the chord (right angle at E, dotted segment). Points B, D, E, C, A in order on the chord.

A.why: Perpendicular from centre to chord of concentric circles.

B.why: Perpendicular from M to chord meets at E, midpoint property in concentric circles.

entries.text: fig (2): two concentric circles with centre M (outer blue, inner pink). Chord AB... a chord through the outer circle labelled D, B on the left and A, C on the right; points L, X on upper part, Y, Z on lower part; segments drawn through M; points A, B, C, D on outer circle, L, X, Y, Z on inner circle.

entries.text: fig (1): two concentric circles with centre M (outer yellow, inner green). Two chords of the outer circle meeting at A on the right: chord from C (top left) through L and Z to A, and chord from B (left) through Y and X to A. Points L, Z on the first chord, Y, X on the second, M the centre.

B.why: Concentric circles with chords, equal segments via perpendicular from the centre.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; parallel chords CD (top) and AB (bottom) with D, C at top left/right and B, A at bottom left/right; vertical line through M meets CD at Y and AB at X; equal-length tick marks on AB at X; arrows on the chords marking parallel.

entries.text: Circle with center M, inscribed triangle ABC (A top, C left, B right). D on BC with right angle at D from MD; E on AC with right angle at E from ME; triangle CDE/MED region shaded green; M marked.

entries.text: Circle with center M, inscribed triangle ABC (A top, C left, B bottom right); angle A = 60°, angle B = 70°; X on AB and Y on AC with right angle marks; triangle MXY shaded blue.

B.why: Perpendiculars from centre to chords AB and AC used to compute angles/prove in triangle MXY.

lessons.title: Positions of a point, a Straight Line and a Circle with Respect to a Circle

objectives.label: Position of a point relative to a circle
objectives.description: Determine the position of a point with respect to a circle by comparing MA with the radius r, and find unknown values (x) from such conditions.

objectives.label: Line and circle; tangents
objectives.description: Determine whether a straight line is outside, a secant or a tangent to a circle by comparing the distance MA with the radius r, and use the perpendicularity of a tangent to the radius at the point of tangency to calculate lengths and angles and to justify that a line is a tangent.

objectives.label: Position of two circles
objectives.description: Determine the position of two circles (distant, touching externally or internally, intersecting, concentric) by comparing MN with r_1 + r_2 and r_1 - r_2.

objectives.label: Line of centers applications
objectives.description: Use the line of centers of touching or intersecting circles, with the common tangent and the common chord, to calculate lengths and angles and to prove relations.

entries.text: Green circle with centre M. Point C inside the circle near the upper left, point B on the circle at the bottom right, point A outside the circle at the upper right. Positions read from the picture; verify.

A.why: Points A, B, C relative to circle M show the three positions of a point.

B.why: Points A, B, C outside, on and inside circle M.

entries.text: If A is on the circle, then MA = r, and vice versa. $MA = r$

A.why: Point on the circle means MA = r.

B.why: A on the circle means MA = r.

entries.text: If A is inside the circle, then MA < r, and vice versa. $MA < r$

A.why: Point inside the circle means MA < r.

B.why: A inside the circle means MA < r.

entries.text: Three pink circles with centre M and a radius drawn to the left-up; segment MA in pink. (1) A outside the circle, just beyond the right edge. (2) A on the circle, on its right edge. (3) A inside the circle, left of the edge.

A.why: Shows A outside, on, and inside circle M for MA vs r.

B.why: Point A outside, on, and inside the circle.

entries.text: Green circle with centre M, point B on the circle joined to M by a horizontal radius, and point A outside the circle joined to M by a pink segment.

A.why: Introduces the line-and-circle activity with MA compared to r, leading to line positions.

B.why: Point A outside with MA and radius MB, leading to the line-and-circle cases.

entries.text: The straight line L is located outside the circle M, L ∩ circle M = ϕ; so MA > r and vice versa. $L \cap M = \phi,\ MA > r$

A.why: A line outside the circle has empty intersection and MA > r.

B.why: Line outside the circle: MA > r.

entries.text: The straight line L is a secant to the circle M, L ∩ circle M = {C, D}; so MA < r and vice versa. $L \cap M = \{C, D\},\ MA < r$

A.why: A secant meets the circle at two points and MA < r.

B.why: Secant case: MA < r.

entries.text: Case 1: yellow circle with centre M, horizontal line through M and A, A outside the circle with right angle mark; vertical line L through A does not meet the circle.

A.why: Case of a line outside the circle.

B.why: Case 1: line outside the circle.

entries.text: Case 2: yellow circle with centre M, horizontal line through M and A inside the circle; vertical line L through A meets the circle at C (above) and D (below).

A.why: Case of a secant line.

B.why: Case 2: line is a secant.

entries.text: Case 3: yellow circle with centre M, horizontal line through M and A on the circle; vertical line L through A touches the circle at A with a right angle mark.

A.why: Case of a tangent line.

B.why: Case 3: line touching the circle, a tangent.

entries.text: Green circle with centre M, radius MA drawn down to point A on the circle; line L is tangent to the circle at A (right angle shown).

A.why: Tangent perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.

B.why: Tangent L perpendicular to radius MA at A.

entries.text: If a straight line is perpendicular to a diameter of a circle at one of its endpoints, then it is a tangent to the circle.

A.why: Criterion to justify that a line is a tangent.

B.why: Converse: perpendicular to a diameter at its end is a tangent.

entries.text: Pink circle with centre M and diameter AB; line L passes through A perpendicular to AB (right angle mark at A), tangent to the circle at A.

A.why: Line perpendicular to a diameter at its endpoint is tangent.

B.why: Line perpendicular to diameter at its endpoint is a tangent.

entries.text: Blue circle with centre M; radius MX = 5 cm drawn down to X on the circle; segment MY passes through Z on the circle, ZY = 8 cm; XY = 12 cm along the bottom from X to Y.

A.why: Tangent-radius figure used to calculate lengths.

B.why: Circle with radius 5 and distances to points X, Y, Z compared with r.

entries.text: Six circle figures A–F for Drill 1 with tangent AB. A: centre M, angle 125° at B, points A, B. B: M, D, A, B, angle 30° at B. C: B, C, E, D, A, M, 50° at B, tick marks. D: M, 6 cm, D, B, A, 8 cm. E: C, M, D, A, B, 60°, 10 cm, tick marks. F: C, D, M, A, B, 3 cm, 5 cm, 12 cm.

A.why: Drill figures with tangent AB for calculating lengths and angles.

B.why: Drill 1 figures with tangent AB to calculate lengths and angles.

entries.text: Three circle figures for Drill 2. A: M, 54° at M, 36° at B, points A, B. B: M, A, C, B with tick marks. C: M, A, D, B, right angle at B, tick marks.

A.why: Drill figures with tangents for angles and lengths.

B.why: Drill 2 figures on tangents perpendicular to radius.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and a straight line L passing through M (a diameter line, extended with arrows both ends).

A.why: Circle with a line through its centre as an axis of symmetry begins the two-circle activity.

B.why: Circle with axis of symmetry line L, part of the two-circle activity.

entries.text: Pink circle with centre N marked, drawn on a beige transparent paper.

A.why: Transparent-paper circle N in the two-circle activity.

B.why: Circle N on transparent paper for the two-circle activity.

entries.text: The straight line l = line MN is called the line of centers of the two circles M and N, and it is an axis of symmetry for both of them.

A.why: Defines the line of centers, introduced in the two-circle positions activity.

B.why: Defines line of centers in the activity on positions of two circles.

entries.text: Pink circle N on beige transparent paper, to the left of larger blue circle M; a horizontal line with arrowheads passes through centres N and M; a red arrow points right.

A.why: Activity figure placing circle N on the line of centers with circle M.

B.why: Transparent-paper activity figure for two circles' positions.

entries.text: Drill part 1: pink circle N (radius r2) and blue circle M (radius r1) separate, not touching; segment joins centres N and M with r2 and r1 labelled.

A.why: Distant circles case, MN > r1 + r2.

B.why: Distant circles case.

entries.text: Drill part 2: pink circle N and blue circle M touching externally at point A on segment NM; r2 and r1 labelled; a vertical line through A with endpoint B at top.

A.why: Externally touching circles case, MN = r1 + r2.

B.why: Externally touching circles case.

entries.text: Drill part 3: pink circle N and blue circle M overlapping; intersection lens shaded yellow with points A (top) and B (bottom); dashed segments from N and M to A and B; segment NM drawn.

A.why: Intersecting circles case.

B.why: Intersecting circles case in the position of two circles.

entries.text: Two circles touching internally: smaller pink circle with centre N inside larger blue circle with centre M; dashed segment from the point of tangency A through N to M; vertical common tangent line through A with B marked at its top. Points M, N, A, B labelled.

A.why: Internally touching circles case, MN = r1 - r2.

B.why: Internally touching circles, a position of two circles.

entries.text: Point 5: If $MN < r_1 - r_2$, then $M \cap N = \ldots$ (blank), surface of circle M ∩ surface of circle N = ... (blank), and the two circles are intersecting as in figure ... (blank). $MN < r_1 - r_2$

A.why: MN < r1 - r2 case of the position of two circles.

B.why: Case MN < r1 - r2 of the position of two circles.

entries.text: When $MN = 0$ (zero), the two circles are concentric, as in figure ... (blank). $MN = 0$

A.why: MN = 0 gives concentric circles.

B.why: MN = 0 means the circles are concentric.

entries.text: Figure A: pink circle inside a larger blue circle, concentric, with M and N labelled at the same centre (a dot). Marked A below.

A.why: Concentric circles figure.

B.why: Concentric circles, a position of two circles.

entries.text: Figure B: pink circle inside a larger blue circle, not concentric; dashed segment from the left edge of the small circle through N to M; M and N labelled close together. Marked B below.

A.why: Non-concentric circle inside another, a two-circle position.

B.why: Non-concentric circles one inside the other, a position of two circles.

entries.text: The line of centers of two touching circles passes through a point of tangency and is perpendicular to the common tangent.

A.why: Line of centers of touching circles is perpendicular to the common tangent.

B.why: States the line of centers of touching circles passes through the tangency point and is perpendicular to the common tangent.

entries.text: Large green circle with smaller yellow circle inside touching internally at A. Points N and M inside the small circle (N left, M right), A on the left at the tangent point, B above A on the common tangent line AB. Dashed segment from A to N/M; pink triangle BMN shaded.

A.why: Touching circles with common tangent and line of centers for calculations.

B.why: Internally touching circles with common tangent and line of centers for calculation.

entries.text: Drill figures 1–6. (1) Circle N inside circle M touching internally at A on a line through B; angle at B is 40°, M above N, arrow down from M through N to A. (2) Small circle N with radius 5 cm inside circle M touching internally; MC = 3 cm, points A, B, C marked, B on right of M. (3) Circle M (radius 8 cm) and circle N (radius 5 cm) touching externally at A; C and B on a tangent line below. (4) C

A.why: Drill figures of touching circles with common tangent.

B.why: Drill figures of touching circles using line of centers and tangent.

entries.text: Two intersecting circles N (blue, left) and M (pink, right) meeting at A (top) and B (bottom). CD diameter of circle M through center M, C top right, D bottom. F on AB at the line NM. Line from E through A, F, B vertical; tangent CX passes through E and C, with X at upper left.

A.why: Intersecting circles with common chord and line of centers.

B.why: Intersecting circles with line of centers, common chord and tangent.

entries.text: Figure A: circles M (green, larger) and N (yellow) intersect at A and B; MN meets AB at D; MA = 10 cm; angle at M between MN and MB marked 30°; MA and MB drawn.

A.why: Intersecting circles, common chord AB and line of centers MN for calculation.

B.why: Intersecting circles with MN and common chord AB for calculating lengths.

entries.text: Figure B: circles N (blue) and M (pink) intersect at A and B; MN meets AB at D; a tangent line at the top-left of circle M with a 52° angle marked between the tangent and a chord/line; angle (3L - 8)° marked at M near D; tick marks on a chord indicating equal parts. Values read from figure; verify.

A.why: Intersecting circles with common chord and tangent for angle calculation.

B.why: Intersecting circles with line of centers, common chord and tangent for calculating angles.

entries.text: If ABC is a right-angled triangle at A and AD ⊥ BC, then (AB)² = BD × BC (Euclidean theorem). $(AB)^2 = BD \times BC$

A.why: Euclidean theorem used in calculating lengths with the common chord.

B.why: Euclidean theorem used to calculate lengths in line-of-centers problems.

entries.text: Also (AD)² = DB × DC (Corollary). $(AD)^2 = DB \times DC$

A.why: Corollary of Euclid's theorem used in these calculations.

B.why: Corollary of Euclid's theorem applied in intersecting-circle problems.

entries.text: Also AD × BC = AB × AC. $AD \times BC = AB \times AC$

A.why: Related right-triangle relation used in these calculations.

B.why: Right-triangle relation used with the line of centers and common chord.

entries.text: Right triangle ABC with right angle at A, AD drawn perpendicular to BC with D on BC, right angle marked at D; points A, B, D, C labelled.

A.why: Right triangle figure for the Euclidean theorem used in line-of-centers problems.

B.why: Right triangle with altitude AD illustrates Euclidean theorem used in common-chord problems.

entries.text: Two intersecting circles, N (pink, larger) and M (yellow), meeting at A and B; segment MN meets AB at C; NA = 8 cm, MA = 6 cm; NA and MA drawn.

A.why: Intersecting circles with line of centers and common chord for calculating lengths.

B.why: Intersecting circles with MN meeting common chord AB at C, used for line-of-centers calculations.

objectives.label: Circle through one point
objectives.description: Draw circles passing through a given point, choosing centers and using the compass, and state that infinitely many such circles exist (equal radii give centers on a congruent circle centered at A).

objectives.label: Circle through two points
objectives.description: Draw circles passing through two given points using the axis of the chord AB for the center, and determine the possible circles for a given radius or diameter, including the smallest radius.

objectives.label: Circle through three points
objectives.description: Draw the circumcircle through three noncollinear points as the intersection of the axes of two sides, identify its center in the triangle, and explain why collinear points give no circle.

entries.text: Photo of a bicycle leaning on a tree, with the two wheels outlined in red circles. Decorative/illustrative for Think and Discuss.

A.why: Bicycle photo only decorates the Think and Discuss introduction.

B.why: Decorative bicycle photo for Think and Discuss.

entries.text: A circle can be drawn (identified) with given terms: 1. the center of the circle.

A.why: States the terms (center) that identify a circle, opening the one-point circle activity.

B.why: General condition for drawing a circle, introducing the lesson.

entries.text: A circle can be drawn (identified) with given terms: 2. the radius length of the circle.

A.why: States radius as the second term fixing a circle, used in the compass drawing.

B.why: General condition for drawing a circle, introducing the lesson.

entries.text: Construction step 1: take any chosen point as M on the same plane.

A.why: Choose a center M to draw a circle through A.

B.why: Choose any center M on the plane to draw a circle through A.

entries.text: Construction step 2: place the tip of the compass at M and with an opening equal to MA draw the circle M. The circle M passes through point A.

A.why: Compass at M with opening MA gives a circle through A.

B.why: Draw circle M with opening MA through point A.

entries.text: Construction step 3: place the tip of the compass at another point M₁ and with an opening equal to M₁A draw circle M₁. The circle M₁ passes through point A.

A.why: Another center M1 gives another circle through A.

B.why: Another center M1 with opening M1A gives a circle through A.

entries.text: Construction step 4: repeat the previous work and note the following.

A.why: Repeating the construction shows many circles through A.

B.why: Repeat the one-point construction and note the result.

entries.text: Four overlapping circles all passing through point A, with centres (pink dots) labelled M, M₁, M₂, M₃: M₁ pink circle top, M yellow circle right, M₂ small yellow/blue circle near A, M₃ large blue circle bottom. Positions read from figure; verify.

A.why: Shows several circles with different centers all passing through A.

B.why: Several circles with different centers all pass through A.

entries.text: For each chosen point (center of the circle) it is possible to draw a circle passing through point A.

A.why: Any chosen center gives a circle through A, so infinitely many exist.

B.why: Any chosen center gives a circle through point A.

entries.text: If the radii of these circles are equal in length, then their centers are located on a congruent circle whose center is point A.

A.why: Equal radii put the centers on a congruent circle centered at A.

B.why: Equal radii put centers on a congruent circle centered at A.

entries.text: Many circles all passing through point A, with centers labelled A1, A2, A3 on a green circle centered at A. Labels A, A1, A2, A3 read from the figure; verify.

A.why: Illustrates centers A1, A2, A3 on a circle centered at A.

B.why: Centers of equal-radius circles through A lie on a circle centered at A.

entries.text: Draw the straight segment AB.

A.why: First step of the construction of circles through A and B.

B.why: First step of the two-point construction: draw segment AB.

entries.text: Draw the straight line L, the axis of AB, where L ∩ AB = {F} (the center of the circle is on the axis of the chord AB).

A.why: The center lies on the axis of chord AB.

B.why: Draw the axis of chord AB, where the center lies.

entries.text: Take any chosen point M where M ∈ L, put the tip of the compass at M and with an opening equal to MA draw circle M; it passes through point B.

A.why: A center M on L gives a circle through A and B.

B.why: Choose center M on axis L and draw circle through A and B.

entries.text: Put the tip of the compass at another point M1 where M1 ∈ L, and with an opening equal to M1A draw circle M1; it passes through point B.

A.why: Another center M1 on L gives another circle through A and B.

B.why: Another center M1 on L gives another circle through A and B.

entries.text: Repeat the previous work and note:

A.why: Repeating shows many circles through A and B.

B.why: Repeating the two-point construction to note the result.

entries.text: Line L is vertical, the axis of segment AB (red, horizontal, B left, A right). Several circles through A and B with centers M, M1, M2, M3 on L; the red circle is centered at O/M. Right angle mark at the intersection. Labels read from figure; verify.

A.why: Shows circles through A and B with centers on the axis L.

B.why: Circles through A and B have centers on the axis L.

entries.text: For each chosen point E on the axis of AB (center of the circle), it is possible to draw a circle passing through the two points A and B.

A.why: Any point on the axis of AB can be a center of a circle through A and B.

B.why: Any point on the axis of AB is a center of a circle through A and B.

entries.text: An infinite number of circles can be drawn to pass through two given points like A and B.

A.why: Infinitely many circles pass through two given points.

B.why: Infinitely many circles pass through two given points.

entries.text: Two circles cannot intersect in more than two points.

A.why: Two circles meet in at most two points, as with circles through A and B.

B.why: Two circles meet in at most two points, so three points fix one circle.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, passing through A, B and C. Line L1 (black, vertical with arrows) is the axis of AB and passes through M; line L2 (pink) is the axis of BC and passes through M. C is at top left, B at bottom left, A at bottom right of the circle. Right-angle marks and equal-length tick marks are shown on AB and BC.

A.why: Shows the circle through A, B, C with center at the intersection of two axes.

B.why: Circle with center M at the intersection of the axes of AB and BC.

entries.text: Construction:

A.why: Heading of the three-point construction.

B.why: Heading of the construction of the circle through three points.

entries.text: Draw the straight line $L_1$, the axis of $\overline{AB}$, thus $M \in L_1$. $M \in L_1$

A.why: Axis of AB contains the center M.

B.why: Draw axis L1 of AB in the three-point construction.

entries.text: Draw the straight line $L_2$, the axis of $\overline{BC}$, thus $M \in L_2$. $M \in L_2$

A.why: Axis of BC also contains M.

B.why: Draw axis L2 of BC in the three-point construction.

entries.text: If $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{M\}$, place the tip of the compass at point M with an opening equalling MA. Draw the circle M. You will find it passing through the two points B and C. $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{M\}$

A.why: The axes meet at M, and the circle centered there passes through A, B, C.

B.why: Center M is where the two axes meet; draw circle through A, B, C.

entries.text: If A, B and C are collinear then $L_1 \parallel L_2$ and $L_1 \cap L_2 = \phi$. $L_1 \parallel L_2, L_1 \cap L_2 = \phi$

A.why: Collinear points give parallel axes that never meet.

B.why: Collinear points give parallel axes L1 and L2 with empty intersection.

entries.text: A circle cannot be drawn passing through the three points A, B and C (when collinear).

A.why: No circle passes through three collinear points.

B.why: No circle passes through three collinear points.

entries.text: Horizontal line through collinear points C, B, A (left to right) with tick marks showing equal segments; two parallel vertical lines L2 (axis of CB, between C and B) and L1 (axis of BA, between B and A) with right-angle marks, never meeting.

A.why: Shows parallel axes for collinear points, so no center.

B.why: Collinear points give parallel axes that never meet, so no circle.

entries.text: The circle which passes through the vertices of a triangle is called the circumcircle of this triangle.

A.why: Names the circle through a triangle's vertices the circumcircle.

B.why: Circumcircle is the circle through a triangle's vertices.

entries.text: A triangle is said to be inscribed in a circle if its vertices are on the circle.

A.why: Defines a triangle inscribed in a circle, tied to the circumcircle.

B.why: Inscribed triangle: vertices on the circle, the three-point circle idea.

entries.text: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle intersect at a point which is the center of the circumcircle of the triangle.

A.why: Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcircle's center.

B.why: Perpendicular bisectors of a triangle's sides meet at the circumcircle's center.

lessons.title: The Relation Between the Chords of a Circle and its Center

objectives.label: Chord length versus distance
objectives.description: Compare the lengths of chords of a circle with their distances from the center, using >, < and =, and find the range of a value from such a comparison.

objectives.label: Equal chords are equidistant
objectives.description: Use the theorem that equal chords are equidistant from the center (also in congruent circles) to find lengths and angles and to prove equalities.

objectives.label: Converse: equidistant chords are equal
objectives.description: Use the converse of the theorem, that chords equidistant from the center(s) are equal in length, to calculate chord lengths and prove chords equal, including in concentric and intersecting circles.

entries.text: Circle with center M; points on circle labelled C, B, D, A, E, F. Chords from A to B, C, D, E, F are drawn (AC, AE, AF in red). Dashed segment from M to X on chord AE, with a right-angle mark at X.

A.why: Introductory figure leading to the lesson's relation between chord and distance.

B.why: Chords from A at different distances from M, starting the length-versus-distance activity.

entries.text: (MX)^2 + (AX)^2 = (AM)^2 = r^2, a constant expression. $(MX)^2+(AX)^2=(AM)^2=r^2$

A.why: (MX)²+(AX)²=r² underlies the chord length versus distance relation.

B.why: Pythagoras fact (MX)²+(AX)²=r² used as a starting step for the lesson's introductory activity.

entries.text: Blue circle, center M, chords AB and CD with perpendicular distances MX to AB = 5 cm and MY to CD = 3 cm. Points C, A, D, B, X, Y labelled.

A.why: Chords at distances 5 and 3 cm from the center illustrate comparing distance and length.

B.why: Distances 5 cm and 3 cm shown against chord lengths in the length-distance activity.

entries.text: Pink circle, center M, chords CD and AB with distances MY (to CD) and MX (to AB); chord CD length 7 cm, chord AB length 10 cm. Points D, C, Y, X, A, B labelled, right-angle marks at Y and X.

A.why: Chords 7 and 10 cm with their distances illustrate closer chord is longer.

B.why: Chords 7 cm and 10 cm with distances MY and MX, comparing length to distance.

entries.text: Green circle, center M, chords CD length 8 cm and AB length 8 cm, with distances MY to CD and MX to AB. Points C, D, Y, M, X, B, A labelled, right-angle marks.

A.why: Equal chords of 8 cm shown with equal distances from the center.

B.why: Equal chords of 8 cm with distances MY and MX, the activity on equal chords' distances.

entries.text: Circle with centre M. Chord CD labelled (X + 1) cm, with F on CD and MF perpendicular to CD (right angle at F). Chord BA labelled 7 cm, E on BA with ME perpendicular to BA (right angle at E). Segment MB... a segment labelled 5 cm runs from B to M. Points C, D, B, A on the circle.

A.why: Figure for the exercise with MF < ME and the range of X+1.

B.why: Chord lengths and distances compared to find the range of x.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; chords AB and CD with perpendiculars MX to AB (X on AB) and MY to CD (Y on CD), right angles marked at X and Y; dashed segments MA and MC drawn. Points C, A, Y, X, D, B, M labelled.

A.why: Figure for the worked proof that equal chords are equidistant.

B.why: Figure for proving the theorem that equal chords are equidistant.

entries.text: Corollary: In congruent circles, chords which are equal in length are equidistant from the centers.

A.why: Corollary extends the equal-chords theorem to congruent circles.

B.why: Corollary: equal chords in congruent circles are equidistant from the centers.

entries.text: Two congruent circles. Left circle centre N with chord DC, Y on DC, NY perpendicular to DC (right angle), dashed radius from N to C; equal-length tick marks on the chord halves and a double tick on the dashed radius. Right circle centre M with chord BA, X on BA, MX perpendicular to BA, dashed radius from M to A, similar tick marks.

A.why: Congruent circles with equal chords illustrate the corollary on equidistance.

B.why: Congruent circles with equal chord halves, illustrating equal chords are equidistant in congruent circles.

entries.text: Drill A: circle with centre M, chords AB and CD (A, B, C, D on circle), perpendiculars MX to AB and MY to CD with right-angle marks; points O and E also marked on the circle (E on the right, O on the left); X, Y are feet of perpendiculars.

A.why: Drill A figure comparing chords with their distances from the center.

B.why: Drill A: chords AB and CD with perpendiculars, applying the equal-chords theorem.

entries.text: Drill B: circle with centre M, chords AB and CD, perpendiculars from M to the chords meeting at O (on CD) and E (on AB) with right-angle marks; segment MO = 6 cm, length labelled (3X + 4) cm along the left chord part, ME = (X + 2) cm.

A.why: Drill B finds lengths using equal distances MO and ME of equal chords.

B.why: Drill B: equal chords have equal distances, giving an equation for x.

entries.text: Drill C: circle with centre M, chords AB and CD, perpendicular feet Y and X (right-angle marks), segment XY drawn, angle XMY marked 100°.

A.why: Drill C uses equal chords being equidistant to find angles.

B.why: Drill C: equal chords give equal distances MX = MY, to find the angle.

entries.text: Drill D: two congruent circles with centres N (left) and M (right); line DA passes through both circles with points D, Y, C, B, X, A in order; N joined to Y and M to X with right-angle marks at Y and X; N and M joined by a horizontal segment.

A.why: Drill D uses congruent circles with equal chords equidistant from centers.

B.why: Drill D on congruent circles with equal chords, using the corollary on equidistance.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, point A at top, chords AB and AC with tick marks, X on AB, Y on AC with right-angle mark, segment XY, MX extended to D, MY extended to E (arrows), C and B at bottom.

A.why: Proving chords equal from equal distances, using the converse.

B.why: Equal chords AB and AC in circle M, the worked example for equal chords being equidistant.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and inscribed triangle ABC (A at top, C bottom left, B bottom right). X is on AB and Y is on AC; MX and MY are drawn from M with a right-angle mark at Y; tick marks on AX and XB, and angle marks at B and C.

A.why: Proof about triangle sides from equidistant chords using the converse.

B.why: Equal chords AB and AC with MX and MY drawn, finding equal distances or angles by the theorem.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and two chords CD and AB. Y is the midpoint of CD with MY perpendicular to CD; X is on AB with MX perpendicular to AB; YD is labelled 7 cm; tick mark on MX.

A.why: Equal distances MX and MY give equal chords, so lengths follow.

B.why: MY and MX equal distances with YD = 7 cm give AB, as in the converse exercise.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and chords CD and AB. MF is perpendicular to CD at F, ME is perpendicular to AB at E; ME = MF marked with ticks. CD's half labelled (5X + 1) cm, MF labelled 2X cm, and the segment on the AB side labelled 16 cm.

A.why: ME = MF gives equal chords to find X.

B.why: ME = MF and expressions in x are used to find values from the chord-distance relation.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and inscribed triangle ABC (A top, C bottom left, B bottom right). E is on AC and D is on AB; ME and MD drawn with right-angle marks and tick marks; angle at B labelled 65°.

A.why: Equidistant chords of the triangle are equal, giving equal sides and angles.

B.why: ME and MD marked equal, so chords AC and AB are equal by the converse.

entries.text: Two intersecting circles, N (yellow, left) and M (pink, right), centres N and M. Line BC passes through A, a common point; Y is the foot of the perpendicular from N and X from M onto BC, with right-angle marks and tick marks on NC and MB. Line through N and M is parallel to BC.

A.why: Intersecting circles with equidistant chords proved equal.

B.why: Intersecting circles with perpendiculars of equal marked length, used to prove chords equal.

entries.text: Two concentric circles with centre M: larger circle (blue) and smaller circle (pink). Points A (top), B (bottom right), E (bottom left) on larger circle; chord AB meets smaller circle at C and D, chord AE meets smaller circle at Z and L. Chord EB drawn; angles at E and B marked equal. Points X (on AB side) and Y (on AE side) on smaller circle with dashed perpendiculars from M with right-angle mark

A.why: Concentric circles with equidistant chords shown equal.

B.why: Concentric circles with equidistant perpendiculars from M, used to prove chords equal.

entries.text: Two intersecting circles: N (larger, yellow, left) and M (smaller, green, right) meeting at A (top) and B (bottom). Line of centres through N, D, M with D on AB. X is on chord BC in circle M with MX perpendicular to BC (right angle mark) and tick marks for equality; C on right end. Y on chord EF in circle N with NY perpendicular to EF (right angle mark); E and F on circle N. Equal-length ticks on

A.why: Intersecting circles with equal distances prove chords equal.

B.why: Intersecting circles with MX=NY-type equal perpendicular distances, used to show chords equal (converse).
